turns.prompt_text: One of my friends says a lot of self-deprecating things. Whenever he screws anything up you and minorly he goes. Oh I'm a dumbass but he like tell him not to be self-deprecating
turns.response_html:
It can be really exhausting to watch a friend constantly put themselves down, even over the smallest slip-ups. Just telling someone "don't be self-deprecating" rarely works, though, because it's usually an ingrained habit or a defense mechanism. Often, people do it to beat everyone else to the punch—if they call themselves a "dumbass" first, it takes the sting out of any potential criticism from others.

Instead of just telling him to stop, you can try shifting how you respond to break his habitual loop.

Strategies to Try

  • The Direct Reframe: Neutrally correct the statement without turning it into a debate or a therapy session. If he makes a minor mistake and says, "Oh, I'm a dumbass," you can simply say, "You're not a dumbass, you just dropped a cup." Keep it factual and move on.
  • The "Defending My Friend" Approach: This adds a bit of lighthearted but firm boundary setting. When he insults himself, say, "Hey, don't talk about my friend like that." It gently forces him to realize that he's being unnecessarily cruel to someone you care about.
  • The "Zero Reassurance" Pivot: Sometimes self-deprecation is a subconscious way to fish for reassurance (e.g., waiting for you to say, "No, you're not, you're smart!"). Deny that loop. Ignore the self-insult entirely and just address the practical situation: "It's fine, grab a paper towel."
  • The Direct Check-In: If it happens during a quiet, low-stakes moment, address the habit itself rather than the specific incident. "I've noticed you call yourself an idiot a lot over really small things. Why are you so hard on yourself?"

How does he usually react in the moment when you tell him to stop putting himself down?
